detail:
Harvard Medical School reports a Mass General study of 55 patients diagnosed with what appears to be autoimmune small-fiber polyneuropathy: people with objectively confirmed small fiber damage, no evidence of nonimmune causes, treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). In the medical-record analysis, 74% of the 51 patients treated for at least three months rated their symptoms as improved, as did 77% of their physicians, and 8 patients improved enough to taper off and discontinue treatment.

The senior author describes the result as proof of concept that dampening the immune system may help this subgroup, and stresses that the retrospective study needs validation in a prospective, randomized clinical trial. The work supports a research hypothesis, that some small fiber neuropathy is the immune system attacking small nerve fibers, rather than a settled treatment standard.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor or a neurologist about what is known and unknown in your case.
summary: In a retrospective medical-record review, Massachusetts General Hospital researchers reported that intravenous immunoglobulin improved symptoms in most of the 51 patients with apparently autoimmune small fiber polyneuropathy who were treated for at least three months, a proof-of-concept result the team says must be confirmed in randomized trials.
takeaways: the study was a medical-record review, not a randomized trial
74 percent of treated patients rated their symptoms improved
researchers propose an autoimmune subtype of the condition
immunotherapy for sfn is experimental; never pursue it without a specialist
title: Could some small fiber neuropathy be autoimmune?
